articles.title: French Word of the Day: Charrier
articles.text:
French Word of the Day: Charrier
Advertisement
French Word of the Day
Members only
French Word of the Day: Charrier
The Local France - news@thelocal.fr
Published: 6 Nov, 2026 CET.
Updated: Wed 15 Dec 2021 12:55 CET
2 comments
Photo: Annie Spratt/Unsplash/ Nicolas Raymond
Add The Local as a preferred source
This jovial word should not be taken too seriously.
Why do I need to know the word charrier?
Because it is very versatile word with a generally playful meaning.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
What does it mean?
The French word charrier, literally pronounced sha-ree-ay (listen here) means to transport something by cart. It can also mean to carry or sweep away, especially talking about a river (la rivière charrie des débris - The river carries debris downstream.) Figuratively, it can also mean to exaggerate or go too far.
In everyday conversation, however, it is often used to mean to tease someone or wind them up. It is a familiar, informal word, usually used between friends.
Depending on the tone and context, charrier quelqu’un can be affectionate banter or a way of saying someone is being a bit mean.
Advertisement
Use it like this
Mes potes aiment bien me charrier - My friends like teasing me
Ne le prends pas mal, je te charrie. - Don't take it personally, I'm only joking with you.
Là, tu charries ! - Now you're pushing it!
Advertisement
Synonyms
Charrier is a much gentler way of expressing the following ideas:
Se moquer de quelqu'un - To mock someone
S'amuser de quelqu'un - To make fun of someone
Ridiculiser - To ridicule
Abuser - To abuse

'Taking the mickey' is nothing like 'taken for a ride' which is the activity of a con artist. Meanings change , sometimes based on persistent mistake or inversion i.e. wicked. "Taken for a ride ' could be the treatment of a victim who was defrauded , duped or conned. It is usually not the loss of a reputation but the loss of assets, cash and similar . The sale of time shares in the '70s and '80s was sometimes accompanied by sleight of hand or fraud. Salut.

articles.title: Do you need a financial advisor when living in France?
articles.text:
Do you need a financial advisor when living in France?
Presented by Arisaig Wealth Management
Do you need a financial advisor when living in France?
Financial planning often takes a back seat when you move abroad as you get to grips with everyday life. It's easy to let years pass without taking a proper look at your finances. But a lot can change in that time, and hoping everything will work out can mean missing opportunities.
Published: Thu 29 Oct 2026 11:36 CEST
Photo: Maurijn Pach / Pexels
You might have had a financial plan in your home country, or the last country you lived in. Left on autopilot, it may not suit your current circumstances, country of residence, tax position, or long-term plans.
Not everyone living abroad has a financial advisor, or even needs one. Some people might manage their investments, pensions, and savings themselves, while others might have worked with an advisor in the past but no longer have an active relationship.
The first question is whether your current financial arrangements suit your life today. It could be that your income, family situation, retirement plans, risk tolerance, and expected investment timeframe have changed and it’s time to rethink your original plan.
Want to make sure your finances still work for you? Find out how Arisaig Wealth can help.
Take stock of what you have
Your country of residence matters, especially if it’s not your home country. An investment or pension arrangement that worked for you while living in one country may not make financial sense after you move to the EU.
Tax and reporting rules can also vastly differ between countries. It's important to understand how your investments, pensions, and other assets are treated in your current country of tax residence rather than assuming the rules from your home or previous country still apply.
If you're not sure where to start, begin by taking an inventory of what you actually own. Identify any investments, pensions, and other financial products–such as savings accounts, investment funds, shares, or insurance-based products–where they are and how they are set up.
Photo: Arisaig Wealth Management
Note what you're paying, from product charges and investment-management fees to any other related ongoing costs. You may find that older products in particular have charging structures that aren't instantly obvious, so read and then re-read the fine print.
Once you've got your head around everything, find out how flexible your existing arrangements are. Check whether you can change investments, withdraw contributions, transfer the product, or change beneficiaries where relevant.
It’s especially important to understand the terms of older products, as some may have restrictions or penalties for changes.
Time for a financial health check? Find out how Arisaig Wealth can help.
Review your investment strategy as a whole, not just individual products. Ask yourself: ‘Does the overall portfolio still match my attitude to risk, timeframe and objectives?’ and ‘Is the portfolio appropriately diversified?’
A financial planner, such as Arisaig Wealth, can help you create a structured financial plan designed around milestones, changes, and uncertainties.
Look at the bigger picture
Existing arrangements may still be useful, and older or less flexible ones can sometimes remain part of a wider financial plan. Changing or replacing them can be tricky, but understanding how they work alongside your other assets can make planning easier.
Cross-border finances add yet another layer of complexity. For instance, you may have a pension in one country, investments in another, and income in your new country. Look at how everything works together, rather than reviewing each in isolation.
Then there's currency. You may be earning in Euros while holding investments or expecting future retirement income in US dollars, pounds, or another currency. That can create currency risk that you should take into account in your overall plan.
Arisaig Wealth provides integrated, objectives-based financial planning that reflects your global situation, helping you make informed decisions with confidence.
Plan for your next move
If another international move is on the cards, factor it into any planning too. Moving countries can affect taxation, reporting requirements, and even access to certain investments. Reviewing arrangements before relocating can help you spot potential problems early on.
If all this sounds like a lot to handle without expert support, make sure to work with a financial advisor who knows their way around cross-border finances. Things can get complicated when your pension is in one country, your investments are in another, and you're paying tax somewhere else entirely. This is where Arisaig Wealth can help, offering independent advice for expatriates and international professionals.
The aim isn't necessarily to find new financial products. It's to determine whether your current arrangements still support your goals and make sense for your circumstances.
Ready to take control of your finances? Contact Arisaig Wealth to find out how their team can help.

articles.title: Inside France: Conflict on the streets, battles in parliament, war in the cinema
articles.text:
Inside France: Conflict on the streets, battles in parliament, war in the cinema
Advertisement
Inside France
Members only
Inside France: Conflict on the streets, battles in parliament, war in the cinema
Emma Pearson - emma.pearson@thelocal.com
Published: 7 Nov, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 7 Nov 2026 12:02 CET
Add a comment
A protester holds a placard reading "generation 6 7 does a May 68" during a demonstration in solidarity with high-school students near Sciences Po university in Paris. Photo by JULIEN DE ROSA / AFP
Add The Local as a preferred source
From the ongoing protests and strikes to the battle of words in the French parliament over the budget - via a brief diversion to Brets crisps - and the warlike trend of French cinema, we look at the latest news and talking points from France.
Most of the focus on France right now is the politics 'de la rue' - the ongoing protests, blockades, strikes and demos, but what's happening in parliamentary politics has the potential to be considerably more dramatic and destructive.
This week the MPs of the Assemblée nationale rejected the first part of the 2027 Budget (French budgets come in two parts - revenue and social security, with social security usually generating more controversy).
The reaction to this, both inside France and out, was muted - partly because it was widely expected and partly because it's only one stage on the complicated and convoluted parliamentary journey that French budgets must take.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
As the EU analyst Mujtaba Rahman put it this week: "Trying to understand French budgetary politics is like trying to understand quantum mechanics explained in Finnish."
Nevertheless, despite being both boring and brain-achingly complicated, the latest steps of the budget are important - the rejection confirms what most people had predicted: that prime minister Sébastien Lecornu has no chance of getting next year's budget through parliament via the normal processes, and will have to resort to emergency constitutional powers, triggering the risk of bringing down another French government.
But this time, the financial watchdogs and hedge funds are circling - confirmation that France is essentially incapable of addressing its spiralling deficit by passing even a modestly cost-cutting budget could trigger downgrades of the country's credit rating, spiralling borrowing costs and chaos on the financial markets that has the potential to destabilise the eurozone.
In short, something far more destructive than burning bins and smashed shop windows.
Advertisement
Street life
But the politics of the street continue - among the myriad protests that took place this week alone - school blockades, a nationwide strike, another Saturday of demos - was a call for young people to join a 'generation 6-7 mobilisation'.
I notice that French youngsters have really embraced the idea of being 'the 6-7 generation' - named after the internet meme that began life in the US - perhaps just because it makes a pleasing slogan to say that 'géneration 6-7 refait '68', referencing the huge student protests in May 1968 that very nearly brought down the government (president Charles De Gaulle briefly fled the country).
But I do enjoy the fact that what began in America as a silly internet meme has, on arrival in France, mutated into a call for Revolution.
Talking France
We discuss the latest from the protests on the Talking France podcast, as well as the plan to ease the doctor shortage in rural France, best cheeses and the town where the most 'perfect' French is spoken. Listen here.
Advertisement
Art
Another thing that protests have over budget debates is better images - below is my favourite placard from this week's demos, featuring the Breton crisp brand Brets. Brets are known for their dizzying range of flavours, from the excellent - jalapeno cheddar - to the weird and horrible (pastis), so here the protesters have imagined two new flavours: 'burning bin' and 'tear-gassing kids'.
@ronanmaenardo.bsky.social la Bretagne toujours sûre.
[image or embed]
— veroservat ( @veroservat.bsky.social) 5 November 2026 at 17:11
There's also a new song doing the rounds at the protests, with the highly elevated lyrics: "On fait caca sur Bardella, on fait pipi sur les Nazis" - we poo on [Jordan] Bardella, we pee on the Nazis, with the most childish words possible for poo and wee, caca and pipi.
It didn't take long before a keen DJ made a remix.
Please note, The Local supports reasoned and adult political debate rather than scatological insults of one's ideological rivals. Unless it's funny.
Maybe if the MPs come up with a song we'll all find it easier to pay attention to the budget?
Advertisement
Wartime drama
It's hard to get away from the sense of next year's election dominating the discourse, even at the cinema. There's a striking glut of World War II films released this year - Les Rayons et Les Ombres in May while the two De Gaulle films, Notre Salut and Moulin are all in French cinemas now.
All of these films essentially focus on the choice between resisting a regime or collaborating with it - De Gaulle of course led the French French from abroad while Jean Moulin led the Resistance within France before being betrayed, captured and tortured to death.
Meanwhile Les Rayons et les Ombres and Notre Salut focus on people who took the other path and collaborated. Both are based on real people - the high-profile collaborationist journalist Jean Luchaire in Les Rayons et Les Ombres and the director's own great-grandfather in the case of Notre Salut.
It's hard to escape the modern parallels - I was lucky enough to attend a De Gaulle screening that included a Q&A with the director, who was very explicit that he had made these films at least in part to appeal to young people and to show them that resistance is always possible, no matter how hopeless things seem.
READ ALSO: ANALYSIS: Why are there so many WWII films in French cinemas right now?

articles.title: France braces for protests as Yellow Vests urge 'mass disobedience'
articles.text:
France braces for protests as Yellow Vests urge 'mass disobedience'
Advertisement
Protests
France braces for protests as Yellow Vests urge 'mass disobedience'
AFP - news@thelocal.fr
Published: 7 Nov, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 7 Nov 2026 07:57 CET
Add a comment
A protestor waves a French flag among tear gas smokes while taking part in a nationwide demonstration over the rising cost of living and inequality organised by Yellow Vest movement, labour unions and high school and university students, in Lyon. Photo by JEFF PACHOUD / AFP.
Add The Local as a preferred source
French unions and student groups are set to take to the streets for another day of protests on Saturday, while the Yellow Vests movement plans a separate rally in central Paris despite a ban by authorities.
The demonstrations follow weeks of youth-led unrest and nationwide strikes that drew hundreds of thousands of workers protesting over the rising cost of living.
They come less than six months before voters elect a new head of state to replace centrist President Emmanuel Macron, with the far right leading in the opinion polls.
Student groups and trade unions have called for an authorised march in central Paris "against the high cost of living and in support of young people".
READ ALSO: French protests - What to expect on November 7th
Advertisement
Yellow Vests activists, however, have refused to join, instead calling for a separate rally at Place de la Concorde, near the lower house of parliament and presidential palace, despite a ban by authorities.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said 70,000 police officers and security forces would be deployed across the country.
"If there are any rioters or looters... we'll be ready and waiting for them," he said.
The demonstrations have been largely peaceful, but there have at times been clashes with police or vandalism on their sidelines, including on October 17, when France saw its worst rioting in years.
On Thursday, hundreds of thousands of striking workers took to the streets across France in mostly orderly protests, although clashes between demonstrators and police broke out in several cities.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
'Mass disobedience'
The Yellow Vests movement, which staged street protests eight years ago against Macron's government over planned fuel-tax hikes, has called for its banned rally to go ahead.
"We are calling for mass disobedience," said Benjamin Ball, a member of its coordinating committee.
Authorities are determined to prevent a repeat of the rioting and looting that marred the October 17 demonstrations, although the interior ministry said Thursday's protests had "generally gone well" despite 642 arrests.
The police response has faced criticism for being heavy-handed, with dozens of internal investigations launched into allegations of brutality against demonstrators.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has said he will discuss wages and purchasing power with representatives of trade unions and employers' organisations on Monday.
Advertisement
"The only thing that will bring the protests to an end is a response to the demands that have been put forward for several weeks by workers, civil servants, young people and pensioners," an inter-union coalition said on Friday.
The unions are calling for an increase in the minimum wage, which has not received any discretionary boost since 2012, across-the-board wage raises, tax reforms and better learning conditions for young people.
With the European Union's second-largest economy under pressure to rein in debt, the government has limited scope to appease protesters.

articles.title: French lawyers to sue interior minister over protester 'mutilations'
articles.text:
French lawyers to sue interior minister over protester 'mutilations'
Advertisement
Police
French lawyers to sue interior minister over protester 'mutilations'
AFP - news@thelocal.fr
Published: 6 Nov, 2026 CET.
Updated: Fri 6 Nov 2026 17:36 CET
Add a comment
France's Interior Minister Laurent Nunez speaks during a press conference at the Interior Ministry in Paris on November 4th, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Christine POUJOULAT / AFP)
Add The Local as a preferred source
Lawyers for at least 18 people wounded during protests in France in recent weeks said on Friday they would sue the interior minister over his responsibility for alleged police brutality.
France has been rocked by high school student blockades and mass protests in recent weeks, less six months ahead of elections to replace centrist President Emmanuel Macron, with the far right leading in the opinion polls.
The high school student movement, which began with youths demanding better learning conditions, has ballooned to other parts of society outraged over the police's perceived brutal handling of the teenagers as well as the rising cost of living.
Rights activist have accused law enforcement officers of disproportionately using force in these larger protests too.
"We now believe it is imperative to target the person responsible for these mutilations and massive damage, namely Interior Minister Laurent Nunez," attorney Arie Alimi said at a press conference.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
He said the lawyers would lodge a complaint with the Court of Justice of the Republic (CJR), the only court able to deal with cases against sitting members of government.
"We are collectively bringing a case before the CJR against Mr. Laurent Nunez for the orders he gave to use weapons which he knows to be mutilating -- which he knows to be weapons of war, which he knows must not be used for crowd control, and which he knows are used by no other country in Europe," Alimi said.
Around ten of their clients have given their consent to sign this collective complaint before the CJR, the lawyers said.
Police blast ball launchers or grenades have caused at least 20 people -- including many teenagers -- to be seriously injured during protests since mid-September, according to an AFP count.
Advertisement
As of October 30th, police had opened 105 internal investigations into allegations of police brutality, according to a source close to the case.
Of those, 52 were linked to the high school student movement, 48 to violence during mass protests on October 17th and 18th, and five to incidents on October 24th.

articles.title: PODCAST 🎧: Tear gas warning, health boost for rural France and which city speaks 'perfect' French?
articles.text:
PODCAST 🎧: Tear gas warning, health boost for rural France and which city speaks 'perfect' French?
Advertisement
Talking France
PODCAST 🎧: Tear gas warning, health boost for rural France and which city speaks 'perfect' French?
The Local France - news@thelocal.fr
Published: 4 Nov, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 7 Nov 2026 07:51 CET
Add a comment
Talking France is a free podcast produced by The Local
Add The Local as a preferred source
Talking France is back with an update on all things protest-related in the country, why it might soon be easier to get a doctor's appointment in rural France, and where in the country locals speak the 'purest' French.
Host Ben McPartland is joined by The Local France's Emma Pearson, Emma Albright, and politics expert John Lichfield to discuss the latest from France.
You can find the Talking France podcast on Spotify, Apple or the French platform  Deezer or on  World Radio Paris. You can download it here or listen to the full episode on the link below.
First, we take a look at an intense week of protests in France and what to expect in the coming days. Then we turn to tear gas - or lacrymo, as the French call it - and the growing concerns over the police's use of it.
We also look at whether the French government is increasingly restricting the right to protest, with several demonstrations having their requested routes blocked or changed.
Stay informed with our essential Talking France newsletter
It's no secret that getting a doctor's appointment can be a real challenge if you live in rural France. But that could soon start to change.
The French health ministry has promised several million additional appointment slots over the coming months, with doctors being sent closer to the patients who need them. We explain how the scheme will work and whether it could make a difference.
For centuries, the Loire Valley and city of Tours has had a reputation for elegant pronunciation, with some even claiming that locals speak the best French in the country. The reputation is linked to historical roots, dating back to the 16th century, when the French spoken in the region was considered a model of good pronunciation.
But is there really such a thing as the 'purest' French?
Advertisement
We've also got some good news for anyone travelling between France and the UK with food in their luggage. The UK and EU have agreed on a treaty that will remove checks on food products containing animal ingredients - including meat, cheese and dairy. And speaking of cheese, we've got a poll on the website asking you to tell us which French cheese is your favourite.
And finally, we finish with gentilés - the French word for the names given to people who live in a particular town or city. Some are fairly straightforward, like Parisiens or Bordelais, while others are considerably more complicated, unusual and sometimes even quite funny.

articles.title: Pet passports: What are the rules if you are travelling between France and the UK?
articles.text:
Pet passports: What are the rules if you are travelling between France and the UK?
Advertisement
European Union
Pet passports: What are the rules if you are travelling between France and the UK?
The Local France - news@thelocal.fr
Published: 6 Nov, 2026 CET.
Updated: Fri 6 Nov 2026 17:28 CET
Add a comment
Disguising your dog probably won't work... (Photo by Lou BENOIST / AFP)
Add The Local as a preferred source
Excitement over the reintroduction of Pet Passport between the EU and UK glosses over the fact that any change will not come into effect for some time - here's what you need to know if you are travelling now.
An agreement expected at the upcoming EU-UK summit is set to mark the return of EU Pet Passports for UK-based pets, allowing easier travel across the Channel for holidaymakers with dogs, cats and ferrets.
READ ALSO Pet passports set to be restored between the EU and the UK
But it's crucial to note that this isn't in effect yet.
A more detailed announcement is expected at the end of November, but media reports suggest that the Pet Passport might return from mid 2027.
In the meantime, however, the current rules remain in place.
Remind me, what are those again?
The UK stopped being part of the European Union at the end of the Brexit transition period in 2021. At that moment, it dropped out of the EU’s Pet Passport scheme.
Advertisement
Since then, the EU further tightened up the post-Brexit rules on access to the European Pet Passport.
The rules are now different depending on whether you live in the UK, or an EU country.
Pet owners who are legally resident in an EU country such as France can still get an EU Pet Passport for their furry friend. That means that your pet may have more rights than you do when it comes to travel (fortunately, you love them).
However, pet owners who are legally resident in the UK need an Animal Health Certificate (AHC), which can be obtained from any veterinarian at a cost of more than £100, for their cat, dog or ferret.
Be aware that you need a new certificate every time the animal crosses into Europe from Great Britain, so the cost for regular travel using AHCs can swiftly mount up for people who make multiple trips to France each year, especially if they have more than one pet.
To get one you need:
Proof of your pet’s microchipping history;
Your pet’s vaccination record;
A certificate for a rabies vaccination carried out at least 21 days before the date of travel.
Once you have the certificate, it is valid for entry to the EU for just 10 days, so your appointment needs to be close to your date of travel. The certificate can only be used for one entry to the EU.
Stay ahead of all the news for second-home owners in France
Once you are in France, the certificate is valid for onward travel to other countries within the EU for six months and for re-entry to the UK for six months. If you intend to stay longer than six months in France, you need to get a new certificate to re-enter the UK.
EU rules state that arrivals from a non-EU country should also have a written declaration that their pet’s relocation is for non-commercial reasons, although this can be in the form of a simple letter.
It's a complicated and expensive system so it's not surprising that pet owners are excited about the return of the Pet Passport - which once issued, covers all trips for the lifetime of your pet (provided their vaccinations remain up to date).
Second home-owners
For a while, some French vets issued EU Pet Passports to British owners of second homes in France with only proof of an address in France (such as a utility bill), but – after an initial requirement that pets should be listed on the French domestic registry to get an EU Pet Passport, it was confirmed in April 2026 that Pet Passports issued to owners resident in the UK or Northern Ireland would no longer be valid.
Advertisement
Since that date, all UK residents, including those who own property in France, must use the Animal Health Certificate.
This is not to say that second-home owners using Pet Passports issued prior to 2021 had been doing anything illegal. But they must now switch to the Animal Health certificate, in the same way as tourists and other UK-resident visitors.
At the border
Tighter border control rules for humans mean that it's more important than ever that the animals and the humans in the group have matching statuses.
The EU's new EES passport controls mean that stays in France are automatically tracked for non-residents.
It is therefore clear at the border whether you are a French resident, and how long you have been in France - non-residents arriving with a pet that has an EU Pet Passport are therefore more likely to be flagged.
